articles.title: Falling short: on Marco Rubio’s second visit to India
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Marco Rubio’s second visit to India this year yielded little in terms of results

The United States Secretary of State’s three-day visit to India , his second in five months, came at a significant time in U.S. politics. Marco Rubio’s Mumbai trip this week was just ahead of the U.S. midterm elections , which would mark the midpoint of President Donald Trump’s second term in office — a point at which the incumbent normally begins to focus on legacy, and possible contenders for the next Presidential election (Mr. Rubio is expected to be one), and start to look for possible partners and friendships around the world. In addition, his visit also raised hopes in New Delhi of a reset in bilateral ties, battered by two years of uncertainty over the Trump administration’s actions. This would include positive moves towards concluding the Bilateral Trade Agreement , reassuring India about U.S. sanctions on the import of Russian oil, preparations for upcoming Trump meets with Prime Minister Narendra Modi at the Manila (ASEAN) and Miami (G-20) summits, discussing plans for the Quad Summit (on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit) that India has been trying to host, and setting a date for Mr. Trump’s India visit. External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar’s invitation also offered Mr. Rubio an opportunity to meet their UAE counterpart, Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, to discuss the Gulf situation and to restore energy security and connectivity. And finally, Mr. Rubio’s visit to the Jamnagar Reliance refinery, led to speculation of some major deals on energy, possibly offering more discounts as he pitched for India to buy more American and U.S.-licensed Venezuelan oil.

Given all the high expectations, the visit was bound to come up short. The optics of his visit to Mumbai and Jamnagar, but not New Delhi, which was announced by the U.S. Ambassador to India , gave the Opposition fodder to question the real purpose of the visit. Despite Mr. Rubio’s two visits to India and more than six by Mr. Jaishankar to the U.S. since Mr. Trump took office, relations remain on edge, with issues on trade, tariffs, H-1B restrictions and anti-immigrant measures unaddressed. Also, the U.S.’s narrative on Operation Sindoor (2025), growing ties with Pakistan, and the Trump administration’s rhetoric on India’s economy, diaspora and Russian oil trade have added to India’s unhappiness. The two sides did not announce any agreements and Mr. Jaishankar and Mr. Rubio did not hold a joint press address. However, as they did at the U.S. Independence Day’s 250th anniversary celebrations in Delhi in May, they attended the “Freedom 250” event in Mumbai. Mr. Rubio acknowledged that while no two countries would agree on all issues, he said the U.S.-India alignment on core issues of national interest was “extraordinary” . From this point on, Mr. Rubio must walk that talk, with a view to ensuring that India-U.S. ties are able to move on from the difficulties of the last few years.

articles.title: In the crossfire: on India and the Saudi-Houthi conflict
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: India must adopt a pro-active position in the Saudi-Houthi conflict

The killing of an Indian national in a Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s Dammam airport is a grim reminder of the dangers the kingdom’s Indian community faces as the conflict between Riyadh and Yemen’s Shia militants escalates. Since the fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis resumed in July, at least two Indians have been killed and 14 others wounded. On Thursday, the Houthis claimed that a yacht with 14 Indians was targeted by Saudi forces near Yemen’s Zuqar island in the Red Sea and that rescue operations were under way. As the Houthis, who control parts of Northern Yemen and its entire Red Sea coast, step up attacks on Saudi infrastructure, including oil facilities and airports, Indians, who are the kingdom’s largest expat community, risk getting caught in the crossfire. With flights disrupted, thousands of Indian pilgrims are stranded. India has condemned Houthi attacks, saying that it “stands in solidarity” with Saudi Arabia. With no end in sight to the fighting and a high possibility of Israel and the U.S. resuming their Iran strikes, further violence and instability in West Asia could make India’s choices increasingly difficult.

The Saudi-Houthi conflict dates back to the Houthi takeover of Sana’a, Yemen’s capital, in 2014. A year later, Saudi Arabia began bombing Yemen to drive the Houthis out. But years of Saudi bombing of one of the poorest Arab countries have proved counterproductive; the Houthis consolidated support among the tribes of northern Yemen and built a powerful territorial army and naval force. The Saudi-Houthi ceasefire of 2022 collapsed in July 2026 after Saudi Arabia recklessly bombed Sana’a airport, to prevent an Iranian plane with a Houthi delegation from landing. The Houthis subsequently began attacking Saudi Arabia’s critical infrastructure, and launched a ground offensive against the Saudi-backed forces in Yemen. The Houthi attacks pose the biggest security challenge to Mohammed bin Salman, Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince and the main architect of the war on Yemen, in decades. Massive Saudi air strikes have neither defeated the Houthis nor restored the kingdom’s deterrence. With its wealth, natural resources, infrastructure and tenuous palace politics, the kingdom remains exposed to Houthi missile and drone attacks, with few good options for a way out. India must prepare a contingency plan for worst-case scenarios. Its immediate priority should be to evacuate stranded Indian pilgrims. It should also articulate a stronger position for stability and work with Arab countries and Tehran to push for a diplomatic settlement to the Iran crisis . For peace to prevail in the Persian Gulf, the guns directed at Iran must first fall silent.

articles.title: Canary in the coal mine: On the performance of India’s core industrial sectors
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Core sector data indicate impending growth slowdowns

The latest data on the performance of the core industrial sectors show the economy may be facing an industrial uptick, but questions about its sustainability remain. Growth in the Index of Core Industries rose to a series-high of 7.9% in September 2026, the second consecutive month of accelerated performance. Any such improvement is to be celebrated, but a deeper look at what is driving it is also warranted. The coal sector saw growth suddenly shoot up to 10.7% in September. The unexpected and unusual nature of this rapid acceleration can be borne out by the fact that the sector contracted by 1.1% over the longer April-September 2026 period. The growth in coal in September was likely a temporary blip aided by a statistical low base and, more importantly, pressure from power plant operators over rapidly depleting coal stocks amid the heat wave. The electricity sector grew 11.4% in September, capping off a half-year dominated by double-digit growth. This surge in electricity-related demand for coal will likely wane, especially since the El Niño factor that drove the heat wave will also result in a milder winter. The other sector that results in high coal usage, the steel sector, did accelerate in September, but not by enough to sustain the coal sector’s September output. The uptick in steel did, however, result in a return to double-digit growth for the iron ore sector, which should bode well for the mining component of the larger Index of Industrial Production.

The performance of the crude oil, natural gas, and refinery products sectors also highlights the fiscal problems India faces. At a time when the crude oil and natural gas sectors have both contracted continuously since 2024, refinery output rose to 10.3% in September. This means that the refineries were increasingly processing expensive imported oil. India’s oil imports in September were up 7% by volume but jumped 47% in terms of value due to the high price of oil. This is set to worsen. The attacks on Saudi Arabia’s energy infrastructure have already pushed global oil prices above $112 a barrel, almost a six-month high. The reprieve from the U.S. on potential tariffs linked to imports of Russian oil provide India a reliable source, but the days of discounts are long gone. It is the time of premium pricing, and each barrel imported is eating into India’s foreign exchange reserves, which are also being used to defend the rupee. Cement and steel are the only sustainably growing core sectors, and those too are based on government infrastructure spending. At a time when industrial output is only temporarily propped up, the government’s fiscal space is fast shrinking.

The unexpected and unusual nature of this rapid acceleration can be borne out by the fact that the sector contracted by 1.1% over the longer April-September 2026 period. The growth in coal in September was likely a temporary blip aided by a statistical low base and, more importantly, pressure from power plant operators over rapidly depleting coal stocks amid the heat wave. This surge in electricity-related demand for coal will likely wane, especially since the El Niño factor that drove the heat wave will also result in a milder winter. The other sector that results in high coal usage, the steel sector, did accelerate in September, but not by enough to sustain the coal sector’s September output. articles.title: Tunnelling through: On China’s export control list, tunnel-boring machines
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Domestic manufacturing and foreign partnerships must go hand-in-hand

The Chinese Ministry of Commerce and the General Administration of Customs decision to place tunnel-boring machines (TBMs) on an export control list reveals a blind spot in India’s supply chain diversification. The curbs include TBMs, walking excavators, and high-altitude wet shotcrete machines. From November 18, if a shipment is intended for countries or regions deemed sensitive due to ongoing disputes with China, exporters will need an export licence from commerce authorities. For other countries/regions, exporters will need to be registered, obtain an export certificate, and submit end-use declarations stating that the equipment will not be re-routed to sensitive locations. While China has cornered around 70% of the global TBM market, prominent manufacturers in the West also maintain substantial component supply chains in the country to cut manufacturing overhead. Further, TBMs are complex to build as they have to be configured to geological characteristics at the project site and perform numerous tasks. Where a suitable TBM exists, it can be used for civilian or military purposes. India has struggled with TBM-related hold-ups with China for at least two years now, including for the Mumbai-Ahmedabad high-speed rail project. Germany’s Herrenknecht AG set up an assembling and refurbishing facility in Chennai in 2007-08. TBM production economics differ significantly from conventional construction equipment as new plants need a minimum number of orders and must be able to access the industrial capability required to design, manufacture and repair specialised components.

However, even though India is one of the world’s largest TBM importers, expecting every sophisticated machine to be produced domestically will send public infrastructure costs soaring. Even now, depending on China’s decision on the TBMs set for India, India may have to redirect its procurement to facilities based directly in Germany or Japan, say, and absorb the higher capital cost. The BEML experience shows that manufacturing partnerships can fail without secure licensing arrangements and access to sustained demand. India should pursue domestic manufacturing alongside international partnerships, e.g., making equipment in the country under agreement with established foreign firms, and develop shared industrial capabilities rather than singular ‘national champions’, as TBM manufacturers and their suppliers can benefit from access to common testing and precision manufacturing infrastructure. Overall, Beijing is systematically identifying sectors where it commands a significant global capacity and establishing export controls to counter western technological restrictions, such as on advanced semiconductors, so any critical infrastructure sector relying on Chinese supply lines will face a compounding geopolitical risk.

articles.title: Peace for progress: on the SCO, regional cooperation, the fight against terror
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Economic objectives can be met only in a stable security environment

Defence Minister Rajnath Singh’s address at the SCO Council of Heads of Government meeting in Tajikistan, on Tuesday marks another significant occasion since Operation Sindoor (2025) when India has used the multilateral forum to raise the issue of terrorism, including cross-border terrorism from Pakistan. He said that regional cooperation cannot be meaningful if countries approached terrorism selectively. Pakistan’s Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar’s presence added significance to the remarks, underscoring New Delhi’s diplomatic challenge within an organisation whose members have divergent strategic interests and security priorities. India has consistently argued that terrorism cannot be divorced from the broader agenda of regional peace, economic integration and development. By calling on SCO member-states to dismantle the ecosystem of terrorism, he reiterated that the threat must be addressed at its source rather than treated as an isolated security challenge. The intervention follows India’s refusal to endorse the joint statement at the 2025 SCO Defence Ministers’ meet in Qingdao, China. New Delhi had objected to a draft that failed to reflect its concerns over cross-border and Pakistan-sponsored terrorism, including the Pahalgam attack (2025), while referring to militant activities in Balochistan. India maintained that such an approach would undermine the organisation’s credibility by overlooking the threat it had brought before its members.

The SCO has the potential to advance regional stability, trade and connectivity instead of becoming another source of strategic friction. Yet, its effectiveness will remain limited if political disagreements prevent members from developing a common approach to security threats. India’s position is not that cooperation on trade, culture, connectivity and development must be suspended until every security dispute is resolved. Rather, these objectives cannot be met independently of a stable security environment. Economic corridors require predictable borders, investors need confidence in the rule of law, and transport networks must be violence- and disruption-free. Connectivity projects such as the International North-South Transport Corridor and the development of Chabahar Port offer Central Asia connectivity with wider markets. Their long-term value, however, depends on respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, alongside conditions that allow goods, capital and people to move freely. The SCO’s challenge is to translate its stated commitment to combating terrorism into practical cooperation through intelligence-sharing, action against terror financing, disruption of recruitment networks and the denial of safe havens to terrorist groups. While retaining its principle against terrorism, India should lead efforts to achieve more regional cooperation in tackling it.

articles.title: Bitter and sweet: on FSSAI draft restrictions, added sugars in infant foods
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Descriptive Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The FSSAI must expand restrictions to cover all added sugars in infant foods

The Food Safety and Standards Regulations 2020 currently allow manufacturers to add sucrose and fructose, provided their combined total does not exceed 20% of the carbohydrates in a product intended for infants aged 0-6 months. In a draft proposal, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has pitched to eliminate this allowance — in line with WHO’s recommendation to have infants breastfeed exclusively for the first six months, followed by nutritionally adequate complementary foods avoiding added sugars until 24 months. While corporations have defended sugary formulations as abiding by the Codex Alimentarius, public health experts have repeatedly described their decision to sell infant foods with added sugar as nutritional dumping. Adding sugar has often been a commercial strategy, as it serves as a cheap bulking agent, improves palatability and encourages repeat purchases. WHO’s nutrient and promotion profile model for baby foods in 2022 also identified sweet purées and products in which fruits released sugars during processing as concerns. While the FSSAI’s draft proposal is a step in the right direction, stopping here would allow manufacturers to replace sucrose with another sweetening ingredient. It should assess the ingredients that manufacturers add and the nutritional profile of the finished food, thus completing the loop, with the Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles, and Infant Foods Act 1992 rightly restricting aggressively the marketing of infant foods for children up to two years old.

Research has found that children who regularly received sweetened water during infancy subsequently preferred sweeter liquids, while exposure to different infant formula flavours influenced their dietary preferences years later, including for foods tasting neutral or bitter. Across both personal and public health dimensions, then, infants need to encounter diverse flavours. Since the 2024 dietary guidelines of the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition say that children under two should avoid added sugars, the FSSAI’s draft proposal limiting itself to six months seems like a concession to manufacturers. This should be avoided since India’s regulatory response to ultra-processed foods is expanding after years of sluggishness. India is currently mulling restrictions on added sugar in foods for the youngest infants, on unhealthy foods around schools, and on front-of-pack labelling for packaged foods. If the FSSAI does not expand its proposed restriction to cover all added sugars and extend it across the first 24 months, and pair it with mandatory, interpretative front-of-pack labelling for all foods, its regulatory progress will remain incomplete.

It should assess the ingredients that manufacturers add and the nutritional profile of the finished food, thus completing the loop, with the Infant Milk Substitutes, Feeding Bottles, and Infant Foods Act 1992 rightly restricting aggressively the marketing of infant foods for children up to two years old.

Research has found that children who regularly received sweetened water during infancy subsequently preferred sweeter liquids, while exposure to different infant formula flavours influenced their dietary preferences years later, including for foods tasting neutral or bitter. Across both personal and public health dimensions, then, infants need to encounter diverse flavours. Since the 2024 dietary guidelines of the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition say that children under two should avoid added sugars, the FSSAI’s draft proposal limiting itself to six months seems like a concession to manufacturers. This should be avoided since India’s regulatory response to ultra-processed foods is expanding after years of sluggishness. India is currently mulling restrictions on added sugar in foods for the youngest infants, on unhealthy foods around schools, and on front-of-pack labelling for packaged foods. If the FSSAI does not expand its proposed restriction to cover all added sugars and extend it across the first 24 months, and pair it with mandatory, interpretative front-of-pack labelling for all foods, its regulatory progress will remain incomplete.

articles.title: Manipur to form committee representing all 36 communities for unity: Yumnam Khemchand
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Chief Minister said the proposal follows a query from Prime Minister Narendra Modi on whether such a committee existed to bring all communities together

Manipur Chief Minister Yumnam Khemchand Singh on Saturday (October 24, 2026) said the government would form a committee representing all 36 communities to promote peace, harmony and inclusive development in the strife-hit region.
The Chief Minister said the proposal follows a query from Prime Minister Narendra Modi on whether such a committee existed to bring all communities together.
Mr. Khemchand Singh was speaking at an event held to felicitate hill chiefs of different tribes at the Chief Minister's Secretariat in Imphal.
The event followed the inauguration of the Hill (Tribal) Chiefs' Guest House at Palace Compound as part of the Mera Hou Chongba Festival 2026.

Mr. Khemchand Singh said all communities have contributed to defending and safeguarding Manipur throughout, as he recalled the Anglo-Manipur War and the Seven Years' Devastation to pay tribute to the sacrifices made to protect the state's land, identity and heritage.
The Chief Minister expressed hope that the festival would usher in peace and prosperity and strengthen the spirit of brotherhood.
Mr. Khemchand Singh expressed happiness that people from the hill areas, including some who were earlier reluctant to visit Imphal, joined the festival this year.
He said the guest house is not merely a physical structure but a symbol of brotherhood between the hills and the valley.
The Mera Hou Chongba festival celebrates peace and brotherhood among different tribes and communities of the state.

articles.title: Andhra braces for very severe cyclonic storm; Odisha activates disaster mitigation machinery | LIVE
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Regional Meteorological Centre (RMC) has forecast heavy to very heavy rain at isolated places in Tamil Nadu's Chennai, northern, delta and western districts

Farmers in Chittoor and Annamayya regions breathed a sigh of relief following the recent downpours, which finally ended a long dry spell in the area. The showers have significantly increased soil moisture levels, breathing life into their plans for the upcoming rabi season.
However, that optimism is tempered by anxiety due to a brewing system in the Bay of Bengal, leaving farmers worried about potential crop destruction just as things were starting to look up.
Farmers in Chittoor and Annamayya brace for potential cyclone rainfall today while awaiting El Niño impacts and a crucial rabi sowing window.
The Odisha Government on Saturday (October 24) activated its disaster response and mitigation machinery as the well-marked low-pressure area intensified into a depression.

Keeping in view the impending calamity, Chief Minister Mohan Charan Majhi reviewed the state’s preparedness and directed officials to prioritise public safety, evacuation and emergency response, stressing a zero-casualty objective.
He said the cyclone could affect Odisha, bringing heavy rainfall in southern and coastal districts along with gusty winds of 70-90 kmph.
Five districts -- Ganjam, Gajapati, Rayagada, Koraput and Malkangiri -- are likely to be the most affected, while significant rainfall is expected in other coastal districts, the Chief Minister said.

With a well-marked low-pressure area over the Bay of Bengal likely to intensify into a deep depression on Sunday (October 25, 2026) before possibly developing into a cyclone, the Odisha government on Saturday (October 24, 2026) stepped up preparedness as part of its efforts to ensure zero casualties with disaster response teams on high alert.

Educational institutions in five Odisha districts will be closed on October 28 and 29 while fishermen along the Andhra Pradesh and Odisha coast have been warned not to venture into the sea as per standard advisory.
Southern Odisha districts are expected to be impacted with heavy rain under influence of the cyclone as per disaster management authorities.
IMD: Bay of Bengal system intensifies to cyclonic storm, landfall likely Oct 28 between north Andhra Pradesh and south Odisha coasts.

The Regional Meteorological Centre (RMC) has forecast heavy to very heavy rain at isolated places in Mayiladuthurai, Nagapattinyam, Tiruvarur, Thanjavur, Pudukkottai, Ariyalur, Perambalur, Tiruchi, Karur, Cuddalore, Nilgiris, Coimbatore, Tiruppur, Sivaganga and Karaikal districts area on Sunday.

articles.title: Andhra Pradesh braces for very severe cyclonic storm; landfall likely between Bapatla and Vizag on October 28
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: Wind speed may go up to 130 kmph, say weather experts; IMD issues red alert for 13 districts on Otober 27 and 28

The cyclonic storm brewing over the Bay of Bengal is likely to intensify into a ‘very severe cyclonic storm’, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) has said. It is likely to be the second highest in terms of intensity. Last year’s Montha was classified as a ‘severe cyclonic storm’.

The maximum sustained wind speed associated with a very severe cyclonic storm is likely to be between 118 km per hour and 221 km per hour. During Montha, the wind speed recorded at Machilipatnam was 65 kmph, while the wind speed this time may go up to 130 kmph, weather experts said.

According to the IMD bulletin released at 9.30 p.m. on Saturday, the well-marked low-pressure area formed over the east-central and adjoining south-east Bay of Bengal on Saturday morning concentrated into a depression by the evening.

The depression lay centred over the same region, which is about 510 km off the coast of Andaman Islands, 820 km off Vishakhapatnam coast, 910 km off Kakinada coast, 1,020 km off Machilipatnam cost and 1,100 km off Bapatla coast.

The weather system is likely to intensify into a deep depression and then gradually recurve towards the east-central and adjoining south-east Bay of Bengal on Sunday. It is very likely to intensify further into a cyclonic storm over the east-central and adjoining west-central Bay of Bengal by Monday morning, and further intensify into a severe cyclonic storm over west-central Bay of Bengal around October 27.

Thereafter, it is likely to intensify into a very severe cyclonic storm and reach the west-central Bay of Bengal near the Andhra Pradesh coast around October 28. It is very likely to cross the Andhra Pradesh​ and​ Yanam coasts between Bapatla and Visakhapatnam ​as a very severe cyclonic storm, with the maximum sustained wind speed of 115 kmph to 125 kmph, gusting to 140 kmph​ by October 28 noon.
Meanwhile, Andhra Pradesh is bracing for the impact. The IMD has already issued a red alert for 13 districts in the State for Otober 27 and 28.

A red alert has been issued for Krishna and Bapatla districts on October 27, and for Visakhapatnam, Alluri Sitharama Raju, Anakapalli, Kakinada, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Konaseema, East Godavari, West Godavari, Eluru, NTR, Krishna, Guntur and Bapatla districts on October 28.
Isolated extremely heavy rainfall is expected in these districts.
The State may receive light showers on October 25 and 26, with cyclone-induced rainfall activity expected to increase from October 27.

Andhra Pradesh recorded no major rainfall activity on Saturday, with YSR Kadapa and Anantapur districts receiving widespread moderate showers. Simhadripuram in YSR Kadapa recorded 81.5 mm of rainfall between 8.30 a.m. and 5 p.m., while Malapuram in Anantapur received 74.5 mm. Other parts of Rayalaseema and south coastal Andhra Pradesh recorded light showers.

Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu has directed the officials to remain alert and take precautionary measures to deal with the situation. He called for a comprehensive plan for flood management and water conservation.

articles.title: Road Ministry seeks forensic audit of its portals after vehicle data leak
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: A senior Ministry official says they have sought the intervention of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology to review its data-sharing policy and suggest ways to strengthen it

The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH) has asked the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) to conduct a forensic security audit of the VAHAN, SARATHI, e-Challan and PUCC portals, which hold various types of vehicle-owner information.
Vahan manages vehicle-registration records; Sarathi handles driving licences and related services; e-Challan records traffic violations and fines; and PUCC manages pollution control certificates.

The move follows reports of vehicle information being sold through multiple apps and websites for as little as ₹5. One Telegram-based channel, for example, provided extensive personal data when supplied with a vehicle registration number, according to an investigation by the security firm Cyderes. Details included the owner’s full name, father’s name, present and permanent addresses, PIN code, and mobile number. It also offered driving-licence details, challan history, FASTag information, a downloadable registration certificate, and a PDF of the driving licence. Vehicle Information App (with 10 million downloads) and VehicleSetu — RC & Challan Info (with 1 million downloads) were the other popular apps identified. The Ministry has now written to major app store operators, including Google, requesting the removal of all such apps.

A senior official from the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways said they have sought the intervention of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) to review its data-sharing policy and suggest ways to strengthen it. The Ministry also plans to audit various enforcement agencies accessing its portals.

The data-sharing policy allows access to data from the National Transport Repository, a central MoRTH database that consolidates vehicle-registration and driving-licence records from VAHAN and SARATHI, as well as data from e-Challans, eDARs (Detailed Accident Reports), and FASTags.

Under the policy, government bodies, including the police, law-enforcement and national-security agencies, may access all data fields available through the various applications, in accordance with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. Meanwhile, private entities can access only selected data fields relevant to their domain and have a daily cap on searches. Data is shared through application programming interfaces (APIs), enabling machine-to-machine access or login-based access secured by secret keys, two-factor authentication, and Aadhaar-authenticated one-time passwords (OTPs). Personally identifiable information (PII) is masked for all except law-enforcement and security agencies. All entities must possess a Security Audit Certificate from CERT-In.

Through an RTI request, the Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) found that 25,314 credentials had been issued to private entities to access VAHAN, SARATHI, e-Challan, and PUCC data, through which 1.708 crore queries were run over a period of 33 months.

According to another senior Road Ministry official, a preliminary investigation found evidence of data misuse involving the Indian government’s Unified Logistics Interface Platform (ULIP), managed by the National Industrial Corridor Development Corporation (NICDC). The finding was based on unusually high transaction volumes, with many entities permitted to access the portal recording more than 50 lakh hits in a month.

According to a letter dated October 19, reviewed by The Hindu , the Road Ministry has asked NIC to audit the access and usage patterns of entities using ULIP and determine whether they accessed data strictly in line with the approved purpose, scope, and terms of access. The Ministry has also separately written to NICDC’s data services arm to request details regarding what due diligence was carried out before granting access to entities, the criteria used to determine an entity’s eligibility, the mechanism for establishing the scope of data access (including limits placed on shared data elements), and the process followed for monitoring and reviewing data access. 🏛️ National & Polity 📅 25 Oct 2026 • IN-APP NEWSPAPER PRINT EDITION

Road Ministry seeks forensic audit of its portals after vehicle data leak

🎯 Exam Relevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes

A senior Ministry official says they have sought the intervention of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology to review its data-sharing policy and suggest ways to strengthen it

The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH) has asked the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) to conduct a forensic security audit of the VAHAN, SARATHI, e-Challan and PUCC portals, which hold various types of vehicle-owner information.

Vahan manages vehicle-registration records; Sarathi handles driving licences and related services; e-Challan records traffic violations and fines; and PUCC manages pollution control certificates.

The move follows reports of vehicle information being sold through multiple apps and websites for as little as ₹5. One Telegram-based channel, for example, provided extensive personal data when supplied with a vehicle registration number, according to an investigation by the security firm Cyderes. Details included the owner’s full name, father’s name, present and permanent addresses, PIN code, and mobile number. It also offered driving-licence details, challan history, FASTag information, a downloadable registration certificate, and a PDF of the driving licence. Vehicle Information App (with 10 million downloads) and VehicleSetu — RC & Challan Info (with 1 million downloads) were the other popular apps identified. The Ministry has now written to major app store operators, including Google, requesting the removal of all such apps.

A senior official from the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways said they have sought the intervention of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) to review its data-sharing policy and suggest ways to strengthen it. The Ministry also plans to audit various enforcement agencies accessing its portals.

The data-sharing policy allows access to data from the National Transport Repository, a central MoRTH database that consolidates vehicle-registration and driving-licence records from VAHAN and SARATHI, as well as data from e-Challans, eDARs (Detailed Accident Reports), and FASTags.

Under the policy, government bodies, including the police, law-enforcement and national-security agencies, may access all data fields available through the various applications, in accordance with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. Meanwhile, private entities can access only selected data fields relevant to their domain and have a daily cap on searches. Data is shared through application programming interfaces (APIs), enabling machine-to-machine access or login-based access secured by secret keys, two-factor authentication, and Aadhaar-authenticated one-time passwords (OTPs). Personally identifiable information (PII) is masked for all except law-enforcement and security agencies. All entities must possess a Security Audit Certificate from CERT-In.

Through an RTI request, the Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) found that 25,314 credentials had been issued to private entities to access VAHAN, SARATHI, e-Challan, and PUCC data, through which 1.708 crore queries were run over a period of 33 months.

According to another senior Road Ministry official, a preliminary investigation found evidence of data misuse involving the Indian government’s Unified Logistics Interface Platform (ULIP), managed by the National Industrial Corridor Development Corporation (NICDC). The finding was based on unusually high transaction volumes, with many entities permitted to access the portal recording more than 50 lakh hits in a month.

According to a letter dated October 19, reviewed by The Hindu , the Road Ministry has asked NIC to audit the access and usage patterns of entities using ULIP and determine whether they accessed data strictly in line with the approved purpose, scope, and terms of access. The Ministry has also separately written to NICDC’s data services arm to request details regarding what due diligence was carried out before granting access to entities, the criteria used to determine an entity’s eligibility, the mechanism for establishing the scope of data access (including limits placed on shared data elements), and the process followed for monitoring and reviewing data access. Officials suspect bad actors were likely triangulating data gathered from different portals and compiling it.

Road Ministry officials said that, following a representation from the IFF, the Ministry has further tightened technical controls and will limit data sharing for ULIP. Government agencies seeking data will now be required to get approval from the Transport Secretary, and requesting officers must be verified through an Aadhaar-based digital signature certificate or video KYC. However, officials ruled out suspending data sharing with private entities, saying it was necessary to support ease of doing business and ease of living.

Government agencies seeking data will now be required to get approval from the Transport Secretary, and requesting officers must be verified through an Aadhaar-based digital signature certificate or video KYC. articles.title: INDIA bloc to hold ‘public impeachment proceeding’ of CEC Gyanesh Kumar, says K.C. Venugopal
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Indian Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Government Schemes
fullParagraphs: ‘After this Public Impeachment, we will hold a Dilli Chalo March against Vote Chori culminating at Ramleela Maidan on November 1st, where at least a million concerned citizens will participate,’ said K.C. Venugopal

Congress MP K.C. Venugopal said that the INDIA bloc is set to hold a “public impeachment proceeding” of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar on October 30, 2026, in a post on X on Saturday. (October 24, 2026).
This move comes as the Opposition is stepping up its demand for the removal of Mr. Kumar from the post.

Article 324 (5) of the Constitution deals with the removal of the CEC in a similar manner and grounds as that of a judge of the Supreme Court while the term impeachment (Article 61) is reserved for the President’s office.

“After this Public Impeachment, we will hold a Dilli Chalo March against Vote Chori culminating at Ramleela Maidan on November 1 st , where at least a million concerned citizens will participate,” said Mr. Venugopal in his post.

Mr. Venugopal has said that Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge has reached out to all INDIA Bloc parties and requested their leaders and members to be present in Delhi during this period “in full force”.

articles.title: Ethanol tender sparks feedstock concerns as rice gains ground over maize
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Updates
fullParagraphs: The competing concerns highlight the challenge facing the ethanol procurement framework: balancing the availability and cost of different feedstocks.

The Oil Marketing Companies’ (OMCs) latest ethanol procurement tender for Ethanol Supply Year (ESY) 2026–27 has triggered concerns among grain-based ethanol producers and sections of the sugar industry over feedstock pricing, allocation priorities and the potential implications for the sector.

The tender sets procurement prices at ₹60.32 a litre for surplus foodgrains (SFG), with a stated cap of 108 crore litres for the first three quarters; ₹64 a litre for damaged foodgrains (DFG); and ₹66 a litre for maize, plus an additional ₹2.79 a litre. While ethanol produced from sugarcane juice, sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses has been excluded, C-heavy molasses-based ethanol remains eligible for procurement.

The Grain Ethanol Manufacturers Association (GEMA) has argued that the tender places a disproportionate burden on rice-based feedstocks, particularly SFG and DFG, while potentially weakening maize’s role as an industrial feedstock.
The pricing differential has also created uncertainty over how procurement demand will be distributed among the different feedstock categories.

According to industry estimates, DFG-based ethanol allocation during ESY 2025–26 was approximately 60 crore litres. For ESY 2026–27, the industry anticipates that the allocation could exceed 700 crore litres.

C.K. Jain, president of GEMA, said a balanced ethanol policy must support viable production from both maize and rice, with procurement prices reflecting their different cost structures and allocations providing reasonable visibility to producers. He added that the government and OMCs should review the pricing and allocation framework.

GEMA has also questioned whether maize will receive adequate procurement opportunities under the lowest-price-based allocation mechanism. It has called for greater clarity on the methodology for feedstock-wise allocation and the role envisaged for maize in meeting the country’s ethanol requirements.

The Indian Sugar & Bio-Energy Manufacturers Association (ISMA) has welcomed the exclusion of ethanol produced from sugarcane juice, sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses, arguing that the approach is consistent with the need to safeguard domestic sugar availability amid uncertainty over the forthcoming crop.
C-heavy molasses-based ethanol, it noted, allows sugar mills to continue contributing to the ethanol-blending programme without diverting recoverable sugar.
However, ISMA has raised concerns over the preferential allocation granted to dedicated ethanol plants holding Long-Term Offtake Agreements under the ESY 2026–27 tender.
While the provision is already in place for the current year, its continuation in subsequent years could hurt the sugar industry, the association said.

articles.title: Data suggests broad-based increase in food prices: RBI Bulletin
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Updates
fullParagraphs: Inflation in rural areas was found to be higher than in urban areas; headline CPI inflation edged up over the months and showed signs of greater generalisation across commodities

articles.title: IndusInd Bank posts profit of ₹1,242 crores in Q2; asset quality improvement and interest income drives growth
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Updates
fullParagraphs: The bank’s bottom line for Q2FY27 was supported by a rise in net interest income, which stood at ₹4,569 crore as against ₹4,409 crores a year ago

IndusInd Bank Limited posted a net profit of ₹1,242 crore for the quarter ended September, up 20% sequentially and trimming net loss of ₹437 for the same quarter in the preceding year. The bank had incurred net loss for the same period in previous year due to an increase in microfinance provisioning and write-offs.

The bank’s bottom line for Q2FY27 was supported by a rise in net interest income, which stood at ₹4,569 crore as against ₹4,409 crores a year ago. Sequentially, interest income declined by 2%. NII for half year (H1FY27) rose to ₹9,254, up 2.3% on year.

Asset quality of the bank improved substantially, with gross non-performing assets (NPA) ratio at 2.73% compared to 3.60% on year and net NPA declining to 0.83% from 1.04% in Q2FY26. However, the net interest margin of the bank slipped to 3.23% from 3.32% a year ago.

Net revenue of the bank for the period rose to ₹6,817 crores compared to ₹6,00 crores a year. A decline in operating expenses also helped push the bottom-line numbers, with expenses slipping to ₹3,943 crores in July-Septemeber from ₹4,013 crore for the same period last year.
Deposits of the bank rose 10% year-on-year to ₹4.28 crores. Advances of the bank for the period stood at 3.63 crores.
IndusInd held provisions of $9,012 crore as of September 30, with the provision coverage ratio at 70%.

IndusInd Bank raised nearly $3.5 billion via the Reserve Bank of India’s special window for foreign currency non-resident bank (FCNR-B) account, which was impacted the contraction in NIM. The bank said recovery in margin related to FCNR-B is expected over the next two quarters.

“Q2 reflects the growing strength of the IndusInd Bank franchise and the progress we have made in rebuilding momentum across the business. Our Q2 results demonstrate that the growth has strengthened, profitability has improved, asset quality trends remain encouraging, and our funding profile is becoming more granular and resilient,” Rajiv Anand, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of IndusInd Bank said.

The bank also informed the exchanges on Friday (October 23, 2026) that the Board of Directors of the lender has appointed Priyanka Sinha as an Additional Director in the category of Non-Executive Independent Director for a period of four consecutive years, till October 22, 2030.

Speaking to the media at post-earnings conference call, the bank said it remains confident of reaching a 1% exit return on assets for FY27. Bank also expects loans growth momentum to continue driven by retail and wholesale lending. Shares of IndusInd Bank Ltd closed at ₹835.00 on Friday, down 1.76%, on the BSE.

articles.title: Government to modify labour survey to capture gig economy, unpaid household workers
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Updates
fullParagraphs: Periodic Labour Force Survey will include additional questions to measure labour underutilisation

The Union government has decided to change the design and structure of the Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) to track digital platform workers and capture engagement in unpaid household, caregiving, volunteer, and trainee work. The PLFS will also include additional questions to measure labour underutilisation.

According to a press release and concept note issued in New Delhi on Friday (October 23, 2026), the National Sample Survey Office (NSSO), under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI), has proposed modifications to the PLFS sampling design starting January 2027. The survey schedule will also change.

A separate Second Stage Stratum (SSS) will be introduced in the PLFS to identify households with at least one digital platform worker. An additional entry will be added to the questionnaire to determine whether any member of the household has engaged in digital platform work during the specified reference period.

“There will be four SSSs in rural areas and five in urban areas, with 14 households canvassed in each selected First Stage Unit (FSU). This revision in SSS formation is expected to improve the coverage of digital platform workers and facilitate more comprehensive data collection on this emerging segment of the labour market,” the press release said.

According to the concept note, a large proportion of women in India spend considerable time on unpaid household and caregiving activities, such as cooking, cleaning, childcare, and caring for elderly, sick, or disabled family members. “While such activities contribute significantly to household well-being and facilitate the participation of other household members in paid employment, they have not been measured separately in PLFS until now,” it noted, adding that specific questions will be incorporated to capture engagement in own-use production of goods, unpaid household and caregiving activities, volunteer work, and unpaid trainee work.

Additionally, the criteria for sample allocation and stratification have been updated based on the experience of the previous two years. “These revisions are expected to improve the efficiency of sample allocation and stratification and ensure better representation of population variations, which in turn will minimise operational difficulties during sample selection,” the press release said.

articles.title: Crude oil sourcing presently volatile; procuring more on landed basis: HPCL Chief
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Updates
fullParagraphs: Vikas Kaushal, Chairman and Managing Director (CMD) informed the state-owned OMC is procuring more on landed basis than on FOB basis and term contracts

Crude oil sourcing at present is very volatile and unpredictable, and Hindustan Petroleum is procuring more on a delivered basis than free-on-board (FOB) and term contracts, Vikas Kaushal, Chairman and Managing Director (CMD) of the state-owned oil-marketing company told analysts in an investor call on Friday (October 23, 2026).
Purchases on delivered basis entail the seller bearing the cost of shipping the oil and associated risks until it reaches the buyer’s port or facility.

“All I can say if you look at crude premiums and landed cost: there are times when there are premiums and there are times when you can even pick it up at discounts. It is a very ‘Wild West’ right now” he said.
Separately, Mr. Kaushal also explained there could be instances of discount though the freights could be very high at that time.
Srividya Venkataraman, Director (Finance) informed analysts that freight costs had doubled between the first quarter and the second quarter.
She observed that shipping costs on a Suezmax tanker moved up to $9 per barrel from around $4 per barrel in June.
Though, Mr. Kaushal also stated that landed price may not be as high as it may appear.

“The producers of oil are also stuck. Thus, the astronomical freight rates that you see: if you strike a good deal, you can get is almost managed on the producer,” he explained, adding, “So, the net back to producers in many situations, especially those who are stuck or where there is stranded oil right now, the net backs are much lower than what is in the public domain.”

The HPCL chief also told analysts that the company is procuring more on landed basis expect in cases where sending a ship is cheaper. He added this is also to avert the probability of a ship being attacked enroute.
Ms. Venkataraman informed that under-recoveries on liquified petroleum gas (LPG) stood at ₹245 per cylinder in October and is projected at ₹327 per cylinder in November.
She added that the total under-recovery for LPG in the September-end quarter stood at ₹500 crores.

Separately, Mr. Kaushal also informed analysts that Hindustan Petroleum has petrol and diesel stocks combined for twenty days. This excludes the crude that is presently being processed in their refineries.

Crude oil sourcing at present is very volatile and unpredictable, and Hindustan Petroleum is procuring more on a delivered basis than free-on-board (FOB) and term contracts, Vikas Kaushal, Chairman and Managing Director (CMD) of the state-owned oil-marketing company told analysts in an investor call on Friday (October 23, 2026).

Purchases on delivered basis entail the seller bearing the cost of shipping the oil and associated risks until it reaches the buyer’s port or facility.

“All I can say if you look at crude premiums and landed cost: there are times when there are premiums and there are times when you can even pick it up at discounts. It is a very ‘Wild West’ right now” he said.

Separately, Mr. Kaushal also explained there could be instances of discount though the freights could be very high at that time.

Srividya Venkataraman, Director (Finance) informed analysts that freight costs had doubled between the first quarter and the second quarter.

She observed that shipping costs on a Suezmax tanker moved up to $9 per barrel from around $4 per barrel in June.

“The producers of oil are also stuck. articles.title: Fresh clashes rock France as protesters march on
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Police arrested nearly 1,000 people as officers faced “an extremely elevated level of violence” from black-clad “ultra-left” extremists, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said

Clashes erupted across France on Saturday (October 24, 2026) as protesters took to the streets, a week after marches that degenerated into violence and prompted a firm security backlash from President Emmanuel Macron, who is scrambling to restore order.
Police arrested nearly 1,000 people as officers faced “an extremely elevated level of violence” from black-clad “ultra-left” extremists, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said.
Riot police squads fired tear gas at protesters in the capital as well as in Marseille, Lyon, Bordeaux, Lille, Toulouse, Montpellier and Nantes.
Two people were “seriously” injured, Mr. Nunez said: one man in Toulouse, who reportedly had fingers blown off, and another person in Clermont-Ferrand. He did not give details of either case.
Authorities had deployed 70,000 security personnel across the country for the new marches, called to protest the cost of living.

The violence came a week after rioting that saw public buildings vandalised, hundreds of shops looted and 2,700 people arrested, casting a pall over the country six months before an election to choose Mr. Macron’s successor.

Mr. Nunez said on Saturday’s (October 24, 2026) outcome was more “positive” than a week ago, with more police on the streets acting more rapidly, conducting more pre-demonstration checks and better protecting businesses.
But there was widespread anger at the government over a protest crackdown viewed as an assault on the right to protest.
Saturday’s (October 24, 2026) demonstrations drew between 4,10,000 and 8,00,000 people across the country, according to different estimates by authorities and the organising CGT union.
The main Paris march had between 1,10,000 and 2,50,000 attendees, according to those sources.

Mr. Macron’s government has ordered police to prevent protesters from reaching city centres, where shops are concentrated, and in Paris and some other cities, partial curfews were imposed in certain urban zones.
The French President had ordered non-union demonstrations be banned as “illegitimate”.

fullParagraphs: Ohio and Michigan, the 65-year-old former President blamed the Trump administration for the rising cost of living, a top voter concern amid soaring fuel prices

Former U.S. President Barack Obama delivered scathing criticisms of his successor, Donald Trump, at rallies on Saturday (October 24, 2026) in Ohio and Michigan to support Democratic candidates ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.

articles.title: Indonesia cuts pipeline gas exports to Singapore by about 9%
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Indonesia cut 15 mmscfd from its supply to Singapore from Natuna and another ‌16 mmscfd of gas from Sumatra, SKK Migas chairman Djoko Siswanto told Reuters

Indonesia cut 31 million standard cubic feet ​of gas per day (mmscfd) from its pipeline natural gas exports ‌to Singapore starting on Saturday (October 24, 2026) to divert supply ​to the domestic power sector, upstream ⁠oil and gas regulator SKK Migas said.
Indonesia cut 15 mmscfd from its supply to Singapore from Natuna and another ‌16 mmscfd of gas from Sumatra, SKK Migas chairman Djoko Siswanto told Reuters on ‌Saturday (October 24, 2026).
Singapore’s Energy Market Authority said the ‌total reduction ⁠amounts to 17 bbtud over a ⁠period of 18 days, which is “less than 2% of our total daily gas demand of more than 1,000 bbtud”.

“EMA understands that ​our importers will ‌pursue all relevant recourse in their contracts for the gas supply disruption,” the Energy Market Authority spokesperson said. Singapore’s Energy Market Authority said state gas ‌buyer GasCo is ready to import more LNG ​at any time and that the country has sufficient energy supplies for national demand

⁠Most of Indonesia’s gas exports to Singapore are delivered via pipeline, and the cuts would account for ‌around 9% of that supply. “In order to safeguard the reliability of domestic gassupplies for electricity generation, effective today, gas supplies previously destined for Singapore are being redirected for domestic use,” said Djoko

The gas is being redirected to meet electricity needs in Batam, ‌Bintan and Sumatra, he said. Batam and several cities ​in Indonesia’s Riau Islands province suffered a blackout that lasted 16 hours earlier this month.

Indonesia ⁠energy minister Bahlil Lahadalia earlier this week said he ⁠would prioritise natural resources use for domestic needs, and review contracts to maintain energy security. ‌Singapore generates up to 95% of its electricity from natural gas

articles.title: Trump casts his midterm ballot early in Florida
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: As for the war in Iran, President Trump said, “I may have to finish it off. Or maybe they’ll make a deal, but I’m not sure. Either way, we win.”
President Donald Trump cast his ballot in the midterm elections Saturday (October 24, 2026), saying he voted for all Republicans in Florida before speaking at a Georgia rally.

Mr. Trump and First Lady Melania Trump arrived at their West Palm Beach polling location at the Palm Beach County Supervisor of Elections office together after the President spent the morning at his nearby golf course. Mr. Trump has been criticised in the past for voting by mail despite his long history of railing against that method of submitting ballots.
Asked if he voted the party line, Mr. Trump, who was wearing an “I Voted” sticker, said, “Very much so.”

Speaking to reporters at the poll site, Mr. Trump again defended an ad from Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy. The ad has faced intense blowback for featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Dr. Amy Acton, who lost custody of her children after her husband, the children’s stepfather, was indicted for raping Acton when she was 12.

Mr. Trump also defended his decision to instruct his administration to file its lawsuit to block certification of the U.S. Senate race in Alaska if Republican Senator Dan Sullivan loses over the inclusion of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot.
As for the war in Iran, he said, “I may have to finish it off. Or maybe they’ll make a deal, but I’m not sure. Either way, we win.”

Melania Trump, who this week brokered a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the ravaged, Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky so that humanitarian aid could be delivered and civilians evacuated, was asked whether she might travel to Ukraine.

In Florida, Mr. Trump has endorsed Republican Representative Byron Donalds, who is running against David Jolly, a Republican-turned-independent-turned-Democrat, to succeed term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis.

He has also campaigned for Republican Senator Ashley Moody, who is running to fill the last two years of Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s former Senate term against progressive state lawmaker Angie Nixon.

articles.title: Houthis say attacked Saudi Arabia, Yemen’s Aden after deadly strikes
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Over the past 24 hours, the Yemeni fighters said they targeted three Saudi airports, including the international airport in capital Riyadh, energy installations, a pipeline and an air base

Yemen’s Houthis launched fresh attacks on Saudi Arabia and the seat of Yemen’s internationally recognised government on Saturday (October 24, 2026) after blaming the kingdom for strikes that the Iran-backed group said killed 17 people.

Saudi Arabia and the government it backs in Yemen have come under sustained attack in recent weeks from the Houthis as a years-long truce broke down in the summer, shifting the focus of the wider U.S.-Iran war that erupted in February.

articles.title: Starshield | The non-state sovereigns
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS) & Geopolitics
fullParagraphs: Elon Musk limited Ukraine’s access to the military-grade network of Starlink after Trum pcriticised Kyiv’s strikes on Russia’s energy infrastructure

On October 14, Ukrainian soldiers using drones to attack Russian forces in Zaporizhzhia and elsewhere started to find many of their machines were losing satellite connectivity. Given Ukraine’s extensive and largely successful use of drones in the war, the anomaly was noticeable, forcing operators to abandon missions.

Experts later traced the problem to a satellite communications service provided by U.S.-based SpaceX, called Starshield. A week later, The Wall Street Journal reported the disruption had been deliberate: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk had personally asked for the connectivity to be throttled. Where the order first originated has been disputed, in Mr. Musk’s office or in the White House. But wherever it did, the fact remains: Mr. Musk was able to take para-state action in a war between two sovereign countries. (On October 22, U.S. President Donald Trump said he had asked Mr. Musk to restore connectivity.)

SpaceX’s Starlink satellite constellation currently consists of more than 11,000 satellites in low-earth orbit that provide Internet connectivity to users on the ground. Starshield uses the same constellation to provide secure communications important to national security, with stronger data encryption; its other services, including remote-sensing, use specialised satellites. Ukraine uses Starshield because Russia’s invasion in early 2022 has damaged the eastern European nation’s telecom infrastructure.

By December 2024, the Pentagon had also arranged for Ukraine to access Starshield through roughly 3,000 terminals. Today, its forces use the service to track enemy positions and supply routes and to intercept drones, with the Starlink satellites relaying information.

Mr. Trump has been insisting Ukraine stop attacking Russia’s oil refineries over his worries about surging international oil prices, primed by his war in West Asia. When Mr. Trump objected once more on October 10, Mr. Musk chipped in that Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had gone too far. Four days later, Ukrainian soldiers felt the pinch.

For decades now, private contractors have supplied armies with arms, intelligence, and logistical support. However, the armies had physical ownership of and control over many of the weapons they purchased. With Starshield, however, the provider continued to retain the ability to change the operating conditions of the ‘assistance’ even after the customer had begun using it — like a grenade launcher that could launch grenades to 150 m on most days but suddenly launched only to five metres on one, because you were not fighting your war the way the manufacturer preferred.

The existence of such an entity is the basis of Mr. Musk’s parastate power. Ordinarily, the decision to stop or withhold a country’s military operations would involve political leaders and defence officials. Now, however, Starshield has well and truly complicated the relationship between public authority and private ownership. Perhaps it was a matter of time.

In 2022, Mr. Musk refused Ukraine’s request to activate Starlink connectivity near Sevastopol, the largest city in Crimea, which Russia has annexed, to enable Ukrainian forces to target Russia’s Black Sea Fleet. Mr. Musk later expressed some consternation about the conflict escalating — a compunction he seems to have lost since, even as his own relationship with Mr. Trump has soared and plummeted. Nonetheless, the fact that the concerns of a single non-state actor could matter at all — an absurd notion in an earlier era — has become a strategic reality. Subsequent Pentagon contracts have sought, at least in part, to formalise the relationship between Starlink and the U.S. military.

Today’s armies, and their wars, increasingly depend on satellite communications, cloud computing, and artificial intelligence, all of which private contractors can develop and package at speed and deploy at scale. Musk’s actions with Starshield last week have revealed that military action had until recently depended, perhaps passively, on the lack of such speed and scale as one kind of safeguard. Now that their importance is shrinking, armies of the present and future must deliberate on what can replace them.

fullParagraphs: Documents submitted by filmmakers, including commercially sensitive distribution agreements, were accessible online, The Hindu finds
A data breach at the Central Board of Film Certification (CBFC) exposed information from applications for more than 500 titles, dozens of which were feature films, The Hindu found.

The leak appears to have originated from the e-Cinepramaan portal, launched nearly a decade ago to digitise the CBFC’s work. The exposed material includes detailed shooting scripts, cut orders and other documents submitted by filmmakers seeking certification for their films to be screened in Indian cinemas. The breach did not expose any feature films themselves, which are usually handled separately.

articles.title: NMC withdraws 2023 rules on medical education standards, raising accountability concerns
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: MSMER-2023 withdrawal removes overlapping procedures, eliminates duplication, says NMC; medical activists say the move dilutes regulatory oversight, will ultimately put patients at risk

The National Medical Commission (NMC) has withdrawn the Maintenance of Standards of Medical Education Regulations, 2023 (MSMER-2023), with effect from October 17. The move has raised questions about how violations by medical colleges will be penalised, and how compliance with prescribed standards will be verified under the remaining regulatory framework.

The MSMER-2023 was withdrawn with immediate effect through a notification dated October 14, published in the Gazette on October 17. There is no single new regulation replacing MSMER 2023. Instead, the requirement for medical colleges to submit Annual Disclosure Reports (ADRs) will continue under the National Medical Commission Act, 2019, and other applicable regulations, the NMC said.
The withdrawal comes close on the heels of a nationwide agitation for greater accountability in the undergraduate medical entrance examination.

Healthcare activists and medical education experts have raised concerns about three key areas that may fall through the gaps with the withdrawal of these regulations: the alleged removal of specific penalties under MSMER-2023, including fines of up to ₹1 crore for specified violations and personal fines of up to ₹5 lakh for faculty and administrators submitting false records; the verification of colleges’ annual disclosures on faculty, infrastructure, clinical facilities, and patient load; and the removal of the specific procedures and timelines for enforcement and appeals laid out in the MSMER-2023.

Bejon Kumar Misra, consumer rights activist and founder-director of the Patient Safety and Access Initiative of India Foundation (PSAIIF), said the withdrawal raised concerns about transparency, accountability, and the quality of medical education.

While the NMC Act, 2019, provides statutory powers for inspections and enforcement, Prof. Misra said that withdrawing a detailed regulatory framework without clarifying equivalent safeguards creates uncertainty over how institutional deficiencies and false disclosures will be addressed.

“Medical colleges cannot be judged merely by their buildings, equipment, or number of approved seats. The real measure of medical education is the competence of graduating doctors, the availability of qualified faculty, adequate supervised clinical exposure, and their ability to deliver safe and ethical patient care,” he said.

Prof. Misra has also written to the Union government, warning that misleading faculty declarations, inflated patient records, or inadequate clinical training going undetected could ultimately put patients at risk. He urged the Union Health Ministry and the NMC to clarify the enforcement mechanisms that will remain in place and to ensure that medical education standards are independently verifiable.

Babu K.V., an ophthalmologist and medical activist, said the withdrawal could dilute the penalty framework. He explained that by denotifying the stronger MSMER 2023 September regulation and retaining the June regulation, some clauses have been deleted.

“Like the clause 8(2)c, which states that monetary penalty not exceeding ₹5 lakh [will be imposed] for the faculty/Head of the Department (HoD)/Dean/Director/doctor submitting false declaration/documents/records (including patients’ records). Further, they can also be charged or penalised for misconduct under the Registered Medical Practitioner (Professional Conduct) Regulations in vogue,” he said.

“This is the key regulation ,where the individual doctors are made accountable and hence deleting it is dilution of regulatory oversight,” Dr. Babu explained, refuting the NMC’s argument that there is no dilution of regulatory oversight.

However, a senior NMC official told The Hindu that the decision had been “misinterpreted”. The withdrawal followed a review by the Commission’s legal team, which recommended streamlining regulatory powers and removing overlapping responsibilities, the official said.

articles.title: A distant Pacific phenomenon may be drying India’s north, says study
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: Semi-arid areas are expanding in north-west India as oceanic cycle ‘Victoria Mode’ affects flow of moisture; this can dent food supply and cause displacement of people, say scientists from IMD and Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology

articles.title: Advocacy group questions Medanta MD Naresh Trehan’s inclusion in panel on pharma marketing practices
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: In a representation to the Department of Pharmaceuticals, the group urges the government to replace Medanta chairman with a member free of potential conflicts of interest.

The Working Group on Access to Medicines and Treatments has raised concerns over including Dr. Naresh Trehan, chairman and managing director of Medanta, in a committee constituted on the Supreme Court’s directions to examine the regulatory framework governing pharmaceutical marketing practices.

In a representation to the Department of Pharmaceuticals, the advocacy group urged the government to replace Dr. Trehan with a member free of potential conflicts of interest, arguing that the panel’s independence and impartiality must be safeguarded.

The committee has been tasked with examining the regulatory framework governing pharmaceutical marketing practices and making recommendations on the voluntary Uniform Code for Pharmaceutical Marketing Practices (UCPMP), 2024.

The group said Dr. Trehan’s financial interests and association with the Medanta Group could give rise to a potential conflict of interest. It stressed that the committee’s deliberations and recommendations should be guided solely by public health considerations and the need to promote ethical practices and access to affordable healthcare.

Citing a 2018 report, the group referred to the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority’s (NPPA) examination of hospital bills across four hospitals, including Medicity-Medanta, which identified instances of overcharging. It also cited subsequent Supreme Court proceedings and assessments by State drug regulatory authorities in Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, and Karnataka concerning high markups in hospital tariffs.
The group said these concerns warranted scrutiny of the committee’s composition to ensure that its recommendations were transparent, impartial and guided by public interest.

While clarifying its support for consultations with a broad range of stakeholders, the group said its objection is specifically regarding the inclusion of a member whose financial interests raise questions about impartiality. Allowing such concerns to undermine the committee’s independence would defeat the purpose of the apex court’s directions, it added.
The representation called on the Department of Pharmaceuticals to reconstitute the panel by appointing a member without such conflicts of interest.

articles.title: ISRO will not be privatised, says chairperson Narayanan
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Tech, Innovations & Ecology Reports
fullParagraphs: Contributions from private companies should not be misinterpreted as privatisation of the space agency, says the chairperson

The Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) is under the Government of India, and it will not be privatised, the chairperson of the agency, V. Narayanan, said on Saturday (October 24, 2026). However, some of its operations will be performed by the private sector on a commercial basis, he noted.
The remarks come amid questions on whether the Union government intends to transfer the agency’s launch-vehicle and satellite manufacturing to private firms.

“Our space programme is 64 years old, we have as many as 56 satellites. But the demand is for thousands of satellites,” Mr. Narayanan said during a graduation event at Sri Ramachandra Institute of Higher Education and Research, Porur.

Highlighting the Indian Space Policy, 2023, he said that the ISRO will handhold startups and private companies to work in the space sector. “The space ecosystem in the country and the country’s economy will grow, resulting in job opportunities. When a Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV) or Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) rocket takes off, 75% of our budget is pumped into the private industries. The private companies are also contributing. People must not misinterpret that as ISRO will be privatised,” the chairperson stressed.

He also noted that the upcoming launch of the navigation satellite, NVS-03, planned for October 30, is going as per schedule and that the launch vehicle was moved to the launch pad on Saturday (October 24).

Talking about the Gaganyaan mission, he said that the rocket is ready and the crew escape system on the rocket module has also been developed. “The environmental and safety system in space has been developed. We plan to send three rockets unmanned and we are working on the first rocket. We will soon test the first rocket and then send the other two unmanned rockets. If all these are successful, then we will send a manned rocket. So far 8,000 experiments have been conducted on land.”
He said that Chandrayaan-4, which will land on the moon and return with a sample, is being planned for 2028.

A total of 455 students received their graduation certificates at the convocation ceremony. As many as 217 candidates from postgraduate degrees and 238 from undergraduate courses got their certificates.
